claims.text: The ball-milled Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co powder is a BCC solid solution.
High-energy ball milling may introduce oxygen contamination into the powder.
SPS at 950–1000 °C provides sufficient thermal energy to activate diffusion without causing excessive Mg volatilization.
Enhanced diffusion at 950–1000 °C drives precipitation of Ti-rich and Al-rich intermetallic phases.
The secondary phases may include Mg2Ti, Al3Ti, or Laves phases.
The precipitated secondary phases are fine and coherent.
The secondary phases precipitate at grain boundaries and within the BCC matrix.
The precipitated intermetallic phases act as diffusion barriers.
The secondary phases restrict Mg loss during sintering.
The secondary phases promote densification through pore elimination or pore filling.
Precipitation of the secondary phases increases hardness through precipitation strengthening.
The secondary phases facilitate formation of a continuous protective oxide layer during subsequent oxidation.
The protective oxide layer is enriched in TiO2 and Al2O3.
The protective oxide layer enhances oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Sintering below 800 °C provides insufficient driving force for secondary-phase precipitation and densification.
Sintering below 800 °C produces porous, weak microstructures with poor oxidation resistance.
Sintering above 1000 °C causes excessive Mg volatilization and composition deviation.
For diffusion-controlled oxidation, samples sintered at 950–1000 °C should exhibit a continuous TiO2/Al2O3-rich layer and parabolic oxidation kinetics.
A sample sintered at 1050 °C should exhibit a discontinuous, non-protective oxide layer and linear oxidation kinetics because of Mg loss.
If oxidation is surface-reaction-limited, passive-film structure and oxidation kinetics should not correlate strongly with sintering temperature or secondary-phase precipitation.
